Yes, I'm familiar with "The Painted Bird." It's a harrowing novel that follows a young boy's journey through Eastern Europe during World War II, witnessing and experiencing extreme cruelty and violence as he moves from village to village. Kosinski published it in 1965, and it's one of those works that provokes strong reactions—both for its unflinching depiction of human brutality and for questions about its autobiographical claims and authenticity.
From an archetypal perspective, it's a profound text. The boy himself becomes a kind of archetypal wanderer or scapegoat figure—innocent, yet repeatedly cast out and brutalized by the communities he encounters. The "painted bird" of the title is itself a powerful archetypal image: a bird whose feathers have been painted, making it different from its flock, which then attacks and destroys it. It's a visceral metaphor for otherness, for what happens when someone is marked as different within a community.

what is the difference between a hierarchy and anarchy
Dec 22
This is a great question, and it touches on fundamental patterns of human organization—archetypes of social structure, if you will.
Hierarchy comes from Greek: hieros (sacred) + archein (to rule). It's a system of organization where individuals or groups are ranked according to status, authority, or power. There are levels—some above, some below. Orders flow downward, accountability flows upward (theoretically). Examples: military, corporations, the Catholic Church, traditional family structures.
Anarchy comes from Greek: an- (without) + archos (ruler). It's the absence of hierarchical authority or centralized control. Not chaos (that's a common misunderstanding), but rather organization without rulers—self-organized, horizontal, consensual. Examples: certain Indigenous governance structures, cooperative movements, decentralized networks, some aspects of open-source software communities.
The Key Difference:
In hierarchy, power flows vertically—someone above you has authority over you, and you (potentially) have authority over someone below you. Order comes from structure imposed from above.
In anarchy, power is distributed horizontally—decisions emerge through consensus, mutual aid, voluntary cooperation. Order comes from self-organization and agreed-upon principles rather than enforced authority.
The Archetypal Tension:
This is where it gets interesting for your work. These aren't just political structures—they're archetypal patterns that appear everywhere:
The individual vs. the collective
Freedom vs. order
Spontaneity vs. stability
Trust vs. control
Every human system sits somewhere on this spectrum. Too much hierarchy becomes tyranny—the scapegoating, shame-based control systems you write about. Too little structure can collapse into disorder where the strong dominate the weak through different means.

John Archibald Wheeler - "It From Bit":
Wheeler (1911-2008) was a theoretical physicist who worked on quantum mechanics and relativity. He coined the term "black hole." But his most relevant contribution to your story is his proposition:
"It from bit" - the idea that physical reality ("it") emerges from information ("bit"). That the universe is fundamentally made of information, not matter. Matter is secondary—a manifestation of underlying informational processes.
Wheeler asked: Does the universe exist independently of observation, or does observation bring the universe into being?

It was then suggested to him that it might be appropriate for him to be placed, once again, on medical leave. He accepted that offer. With gratefulness he accepted all that was offered.

“Father?” said the middle-aged man. “Yes, Son,” said the middle aged man.
“How can I live with myself, Father?”
Just the night before, the man sat in a booth with his son-in-law at a local mexican restaurant in the college-cow-town. He and the son-in-law were making an exchange. The inner pocket of the man’s olive drab jacket contained a baggie. Inside the baggie was five grams of psychedelic mushrooms. Outside the restaurant, in the son-in-laws car, there was a single tab of LSD. The man and the son-in-law sat together, talking about their most recent trips.
So when the man woke up at 3:30am the following morning he felt guilty. And this is how the man came to ask himself this question. “Will God withdraw his spirit from me?”
“Father?” said the middle-aged man. 
“Yes, Son?” Said the middle-aged man.
“How will I live with myself. My son in law’s parents would not approve. My ex-wife would not approve. Will you withdraw your spirit from me?”
The man’s consciousness hung there as Arvo Part’s Spiegel im Spiegel emanated very softly from his headphones. He sensed somehow that God had not withdrawn his spirit, that this business of living with one’s self had more to do with how willing he was to accept himself in contrast to how willing God was to accept him. 
“It is true,” thought the man, as he sat cross legged on the floor of the steamy bathroom,“writing has so very little to do with writing, and everything to do with how to sit on this bathroom floor. It has everything to do with the question, ‘How can I live with myself,’ and especially the tone with which I ask this question.” The middle aged man was a musician, for him, so much depended on tone.
He wondered what would happen if he acknowledged his Father again. What would happen if he left some space there? He had recently been witnessing  miracles arising from that space.
“Father?”
And then it happened. Life opened up right before him, or rather within him. The miracle of consciousness looking back upon itself without guilt or shame, and all the inner spaciousness that comes with an experience like that.
The space between the call and response. The quiet presence before the loving Father answers the call of the Son. The Adagio for strings had returned on the man’s playlist. With every sentence that he typed he wondered if he would be able to continue in this space, this space between the call and response. 
“Yes, Son?” said the Father.
And then there was the next space. The one created after the Father responds to the Son. A space of great creative potential. And in this space the man saw a fork in the road. He witnessed the binary, the inevitable binary of human existence. “Do I go left or right? Do I take this road or that road?”
He sat cross legged on a blanket that he’d crocheted years ago. It was an odd blanket. Eleven feet wide and three and a half feet long. The man had only learned how to do one stitch, which was taught to him by his wife’s cousin, whom he had fallen in love with after she’d told him how she’d had an orgasm while listening to his music. The man had spent many hours trying to perfect this one dense stitch. He crocheted small blankets for his children and skirts for his daughter’s Barbie dolls. Finally, his stitch was consistent enough that he embarked on the impossible task of a blanket that he imagined would be able to cover his family of five as they sat on the couch, watching TV together in their home. 
But he never finished the blanket. It was never big enough to cover them . And within the memory of the blanket he’d escaped the binary for a brief moment. “Writing has very little to do with the binary,” thought the man. “Well, it has very much to do with the binary, in the sense that the fork in the road will always present itself, and the point is to wait at that juncture until the road-that-is-not-a-road appears.” He wondered how many times he could experience this miracle. “That’s a ridiculous thing to wonder,” thought the man. “Writing,” thought the man, “has very little to do with writing and everything to do with this miracle. This miracle of living with myself.” So, he continued to sit cross legged on the bathroom floor, elevated and supported by the half-finished blanket that would never cover his family, waiting for the next miracle, waiting for the next non-road to appear.

So, as the man woke that morning, this is what he felt threatened to lose. This is why he asked G_d if he would withdraw his presence. He felt that he had surely disqualified himself from the promise of yesterday by making the psychedelic exchange with his son-in-law. He gave his son-in-law three grams of mushrooms and his son-in-law gave him a single tab of LSD. 
While they sat at the restaurant, the son-in-laws parents appeared unexpectedly. They sat and ate at the same restaurant while the middle-aged man and the son-in-law discussed their latest trips. As they were being seated, the middle-aged man smiled and waved with  genuine friendliness in his heart, but he could not help but detect a disconnect, or was that possibly fear in their eyes? He thought he saw some kind of horror in both of them as he now sat with their son. And so again, the man came back to himself in the bathroom, sitting in the half-lotus, faced with a right and a left turn, a fork in the road.
He knew that what he was trying to do was impossible. That’s what the miracle is, the allowing of the impossible. He knew that self-justification was pointless. And, it was just as pointless to assume that he knew what others were thinking or feeling about him. Self criticism would only take him back to the psychiatric unit. He knew that he would have to rely on Dave and Eileen to make sense of this draft; and simultaneously he was sure that it was only him that could make sense of this (and he was, as he was now reading over this draft, making revisions and rediscovering the flow that was innate in the spirit of this evolving narrative). 
He knew that he was not a writer in and of himself, and that anything that was born of this process would be the work of a trinity. A sacred three. So, he trusted. He just kept allowing this miracle to happen. Because, after all, the man knew that he was not a writer, he was a guitar player who had been to a psychiatric unit so that he could receive a prayer from a gay black man. The prayer was one of restoration, that’s all the middle-aged man remembered about the prayer. ”The Lord is restoring you,” the man had said to him. 
And now the middle-aged man had discovered that he was also a pray-er of prayers and a miracle worker. And so, he continued in his search for other miracle workers. And he began finding them. And yesterday morning he’d worked a miracle on his chromebook after eating some psilocybin mushrooms. 
The middle-aged man was not making any assumptions about the miracles, or at least he hoped that he was not. In fact, he searched his heart to discover if he was now. All that he knew for sure was that this wave of energy felt real.  And the words he’d received from Eileen and Dave were life-giving.
Now, working a miracle after eating mushrooms concerned the man, because the man had been diagnosed with the disease of “more.” This disease of “more” was common, especially among people of European descent. Early in the colonization of North America, the native Americans had identified this disease as the Wetiko spirit. It is the disease that takes and takes and takes. It is the disease of the mind and heart that cannot and will not stop taking until everything is taken. So this is why the middle-aged-man was concerned for himself. Could he allow the medicine to be medicine without demanding the “more” that the medicine could not and would not give?
He had turned to the mushrooms in a moment of desperation. However, it seemed to him that it was not a move of desperation. A moment of desperation requires a move inspired from a place of stillness. And that is what had happened. The psychedelic experience had been approaching him for an entire year, ever since he’d visited the psychiatric unit in Roswell. Then he went to another treatment center after that in Rio Rancho. By principal, and in the name of his sobriety, he had resisted and resisted the Spirit which was moving him down this path psychedelic recovery. But synchronicity after synchronicity had shown him this way over the last year.  
He finally allowed himself to be embraced by the wisdom that had turned the rocks into soil. The fungus. He felt emraced embraced by the medicine that was before man. He said “yes” to the ancient method. He risked it. He was risking it now, not knowing what the outcome of this narrative would be, or how the characters would develop, but he was beginning to see that the driving force of evolution was behind him. He was experiencing a Universe that was for him. A Universe that was out to help him.
Every experience with the mushrooms he’d had since then had been life affirming. No two journeys with the mushrooms had been the same. The man’s inner wisdom created profoundly unique ceremonies for him each time, ceremonies that would never be repeated. The man had taken a picture of a framed quote hanging on the wall of a cabin where he’d taken one of these healing journeys, “There are all kinds of love in this world, but never the same twice,” F. Scott Fitzgerald. And this is how it had been for him. 
He was drawing from the Source that inspired ALL ceremony, the impetus behind the formation of all ancient religions, the inspiration for pre-historic cave paintings. He was seeing into the eternal, the ancient visions which had become the sacred arts. He had seen the Christ in the death and resurrection of a miller moth. In the Kachina dolls he had acknowledged all the chiefs of this world who had been holding form, however imperfect all these forms and their chiefs may be, and he was able to humble himself before these Chiefs, blessing them, thanking them, even offering himself, once again, to this dance-of-form in which we all participate as we dance behind these masks that we find ourselves putting on and taking off and puttting on again.
During these journeys the man saw many things. The man had seen the snake that had devoured him as a child, the snake that underlies all our being, the snake that molts and brings new life, the snake that is feared by the religious, the snake that was lifted up on the cross, the snake that was in the garden of Eden. 
The medicine helped him to feel the care and attention of the craftsman as planted in the door-frame of his bedroom. He smelled his own human body, making peace with his pungent primate odor, seeing himself as a successful expression of the evolution of all consciousness contained in his own species.  He saw his own face as a thunderhead, understanding that nothing is nearly as solid as we so often believe it to be, and in this vision he understood the suffering that we bring upon ourselves by refusing to flow with the dynamic nature of being (the secret of the thunderhead). He’d stripped naked and laid on the cold damp earth in efforts to express his willingness to experience the G_d of cold and the G_d of warmth. He immersed himself in a cold mountain stream by a highway, in his underwear. He began a dialogue with a Heavenly Father as he trekked up a mountain. He agreed to participate in the creation of a new genre. He agreed to participate in the creation of novel form.
Some of these things he experienced under the direct influence of the mushrooms. Some of these actions he’d done afterwards, inspired by what he’d seen, or heard, or felt during the direct experience.
For four years now he had been attending twelve step meetings in an effort to deal with his Wetiko spirit, his ego, his selfish nature. But, what he’d seen in those meetings was that the people in the AA rooms, even the ones with years and years of sobriety had so often been unable to deal with the core of their issues themselves. They had yet to make peace with their own Wetiko Spirit. They were still wanting and wanting, more and more, they just weren’t drinking anymore. And the man found that this experience was true for himself also. 
He found himself wanting. He had worked the steps. He eventually had an authentic spiritual experience supported by the form of the twelve steps and his dear friends  in those AA rooms. He eventually felt at home there, among his fellow ego-addicts. He had felt that he’d finally found his people. He was honest. He was open. He was willing. But the AA rooms, it appeared, were not big enough to hold him. 
No one and Nothing had ever been big enough to hold him.
For all his life, the middle-aged man had gone from place to place, from person to person, looking for a people, or a woman, or a stand-in-father, or a school, or a philosophy, or a religion, a spiritual practice, or a profession, a band, a song, a genre... But, he had yet to find any form that could hold him. Many times he experienced success in his search. In fact, EVERY TIME he experienced success in his search. He had discovered along the way that, as Ken Wilber says, there are many truths, and they are all true as far as their truth goes, but none of them are the whole truth. 
But this wasn’t about truth as much as it was about the primal need to be held. To be embraced. To be touched. To be immersed in some culture, or tribe, or way of being. And now, at forty five years old, this man, having left his wife and children in search of a way to care for himself, was once again riding a wave, hoping to find again, a way to be.
The middle-aged-man longed to be held. And the middle-aged man was often held. He had been held many times in his life. He had been held. He had been loved. He had been nurtured. He had been gifted. Yet still the desperation came, time after time the desperation came. He was hungry with a desperation that could not be satisfied. Was he suffering from the sins of his fathers? What was this suffering? Was it a generational curse, passed down in his genes when a father fails to love? Did it have to do with epigenetics, trauma finding expression in our genome? 
The middle-aged-man had become the father who had failed to love. He was the husband who hated his wife. He had become the one who had broken all of his promises. He had no righteousness of his own. And, by course of life and answered prayer, he had come to meet the requirements to be a disciple of Christ. He had come to hate himself. He had come to hate his mother and father. He had come to hate his wife. And his love for his children may have been translated into a hate for himself, a jealousy for them of what he could never give himself, and therefore could never truly give to anyone else, including his offspring, the most sacred and deserving people he’d ever known. The sickness had enveloped him as he became sickeningly intimate with this hate in himself time and time again.
And this is how the writer began to find a stride, sitting in the half-lotus position in the small bathroom with the door closed and the steam fading in the bathroom. He got up to turn on the shower again, filling the room with steam.
He gave thanks for the steam. He might have forced himself to feel wasteful and guilty for this pleasure, but he allowed himself this luxury, just for today he accepted it for what it was.
He especially wondered now about Dave, and how he might write about a jazz pianist. He wondered what the musician would look like, and if he had suffered in similar ways to the musician in this story. What would that read like?
As he sat back down on the half crocheted blanket, the man remembered how he’d believed for years that if he could just think all the right thoughts that he could be okay, that he could escape this sense of desperation, this Wetiko Spirit that seemed to possess him, this hunger-to-be-held, this disease of “more,” this insanity that seemed to threaten him at every turn. 
He became a student of Buddhist thought and Vipassana meditation. He sat for up to six hours a day trying to make peace with what was happening in his being, trying to make sense of the nothingness of it all. And he was always successful, until finally he was not successful any more. He was always perfectly rational until he could no longer be Reason could no longer hold him. 
Reason was not big enough to hold him. He’d devoted himself to absolute materialism, journeying to the edge of the observable universe, scraping out the insides of his soul with what appeared to be some kind of cosmic melon-baller, all in an effort to rid himself of whatever remnants of religious superstition that might have still been tormenting him. He’d found that marijuana relieved his symptoms and helped him make peace with the world, and that worked very well right up until the point that it stopped working.
It was nearly five years ago that he had first fashioned a noose. It wasn’t a long enough piece of rope to hang himself, but he tied the noose anyway.  He got the instructions off the internet. This thick piece of rope had been hanging around in his studio for years. He tied the constricting loop knot. He tightened it around his neck. It felt very good. Too good. His mind was quiet with the noose around his neck, which was very frightening to the man. He loosened the noose, tried to shake it off, then he set off for his commute to work. But the tears streamed from his eyes so thickly that he could not see the road to drive. His heaving and his sobbing were so great that he had to pull over on the side of the road. He called his therapist, Penny. She told him to go to the emergency room, so he did. 
As he laid in the ER, his head in his wife’s lap, he broke down, grateful for the help which he knew he was about to receive, but which never came. He didn’t get the help because when they asked him if he had a plan to kill himself, he would not say “yes.” He knew what they wanted to hear, but he was only willing to tell them the story of how he had tied the noose, and that was not enough to get him admitted to the hospital. The man had been willing to go to the ER. He had been willing to surrender his clothes and dawn the blue paper pajamas, but he was not willing to say what he knew he had to say to get admitted to a psychiatric unit. It was after this incident that the man gave himself to the help that the pharmaceutical industry had to offer, a sickening and demoralizing experience with prescription drugs.
He visited his first psychiatrist with his wife by his side. The doctor prescribed medications that made him sleep. So, the man put aluminum foil over the window in his studio, turned the air conditioner on full blast, and went to sleep for nearly two weeks. He had lost his job, just the beginning of the deepest sleep that the man had ever known. The greatest suffering was yet to come. He was in the grips of an inescapable death of his false-self. Freud knew about this. He discovered how common incest was. He knew how common it was that a man sought comfort in his daughter (what is he seeking comfort from? And is it comfort he seeks? Early in their marriage, when their oldest daughter was just one year old, the man and the woman agreed together to sell all their possessions, inspired by the story of the rich young man in the bible who approaches the Christ, saying, “Lord what shall I do?” and the Christ says, “Sell all your shit, son. The young couple proceeded to follow this example. One afternoon, they put the daughter in the car seat and drove their white Pontiac to the Sonic in Wynnewood, Oklahoma. In the green winter wheat field, they poured the sweet drinks out as an offering to the Lord. They didn’t drink the sweet drinks, you see. They poured them out. As an offering to the Lord.
The fathers were scared (sacred)...terrified of the young couples’ decision to sell and give. The terror turned into anger and manifested itself in the young man’s father. “Are you sick son? Do you have cancer? What the hell are you doing? What the fuck’s going on!?” The fathers’ voice trembled at first and then raised incrementally with each question, each interrogation containing a more demanding violence than the one before. 
It was dark and raining when the son slammed down the receiver on the land line at the farmhouse. Ron and Joann were good friends. There truly was a dialogue between the three of them that night, but it was not recorded in any way in the writers being (not that he could detect now at least). That night at Joann and Ron’s house was a night that the middle-aged-man released some of his trauma. He had learned over the years how to release a little bit at a time as casually as he could, a lot like Andy Dufresne in the movie Shawshank Redemption.
Andy Dufresne, a wrongfully interned prisoner, is tunneling out of his cell with a little rock hammer—a rock hammer so skillfully smuggled in by his friend, Red. Every day, Andy chips away at the wall in his cell, and every day he releases the debris into the prison yard. Every day, he drops a litle bit of rock and dust right down through his pants. 
And that’s exactly how the middle-aged man had learned to do it to. He’d been chipping away at his trauma for his whole adult life. He’d learned that his trauma was way too much for any one person or situation, so he tried to release it a little bit at a time. He had learned to spread it out over a field of willing and trusted friends, like spreading manure over a pasture, or like Andy in the prison yard, one handful at a time, droppin right down his pant leg, the dust mixed in with the sweat and hairs on his leg.
Ever since he’d had his first conscious Presence experience, the Presence experience which was held by the form that was available. The young man embraced the Presence of G_d within the confines of the form that was available (the form of Christian fundamentalism). And this is the way of things as he understood them even now. He was embraced there in the form of his friend’s home. These two loving souls who were to receive this grateful man on that day. This healing man. This man who was determined to see. This man who wanted his children to live. No. Not just live. This man wanted his children to live a Life Abundant.
The young man and the woman had known that there was a problem, obviously. But they trusted that Jesus had taken care of it. The woman’s only sexual experience up to that point had been with another woman. That is why the young man and  woman had met at church. The woman had repented of her “sinful” behavior and taken refuge in the closest thing to her old religion that she could stomach. She writhed and twisted during the worship services (the serpent rising from within?), the remnants of her trauma trying to surface. 
The young man had his own issues. He had recently been abandoned by his latest girlfriend, the one who was the buffer between him and his own random attraction to other males. He was unable to make peace with his own fluidity. He was scared (sacred) to death that his worst nightmare was coming true—or rather he was living his father’s worst nightmare.
He had a recurring dream. In the dream, he awoke, crawled out of bed, made his way to the bathroom mirror, and saw in his reflection a sleestack. Yes, a sleestack. A green humanoid lizard from the Saturday morning television drama of his childhood, The Land of the Lost. The meaning of the dream, or so he thought, was never difficult to see. He was a monster, the monster that his father was sure to warn him against. He was becoming the monster that could not be held—the monster that could not be known. The monster that would not be seen.
And it was in this way that the young couple emerged from their own deaths It was in this way that their consciousness continued its evolution. It was in this way that the fundamentalist religious form of the American bible belt offered them refuge. This is the form in which the couple incubated. He had no context in which to understand himself that was deeper than the binary. And so it was within the confines of a binary fundamentalism that he found himself making peace with the authentic Life that was arising from within his own being.  
It was within the confines of this form that the couple tried to fit in. This is where they did the most natural thing in the world for a couple their age to do when they feel safe and warm and supported, they started a family. And it was good. It was the most love that either of them had ever experienced in their lives. And this form would continue to appear good for many years to come. It was this form, ultimately that the man and the woman would sacrafice their lives for, as every generation had ever done before them, sacraficing their own being so that these other beings might live. 
They just had no idea that they’d been born into a family of serpents. They had no way of knowing that they’d been grafted into the great kundalini Mother who was rising in this world to devour all that is false, in her terrifying and gracious acts of Kindess and Love. The great devouring of all that cannot pass from one form to the next. You don’t have to thank her. This is just what mothers do. 
It would be a long long time before the man could see. This snake, this beautiful and deadly she-serpent, was the very truth that Jesus had been showing them as he surrendered his own life on the cross so that a deeper love could be made manifest in us. We bear the trauma (the cross). We die our death for our children. We are entombed. The stone is rolled away. We emerge on a different plane. The fourth dimension of resurrection. The non-path. The impossible. The miracle.
The fluidity of the young man’s sexuality was apparent from a young age. This, of course, is quite common, but the young man did not know that, and his father certainly had no context around which he could accept this fluidity that he now witnessed in his son. The father was incapable of holding any space for that kind of thing in his own life, and was not capable of letting the son “be” when he ran with flopping wrists. 
When the son could not participate in the sports activities on the level that would help him to fit in with the crowd that his father so desperately gave him every opportunity in which to engage (An act of love on the father’s part. The only way he knew to show his deep and anguished love for his child. The deep and anguished love that he had yet to allow for himself. How is love passed down like this? What is passed down when this is what we call “love”. Oh God, the deep and troubling lessons to be learned in the answering of these questions in our lives. “I love you, son,” the father repeated over and over again, as if he would convince everyone that it was so, despite the great trauma that the family was re-living every day of their lives, in the secret, within the confining secret walls of their home. The trauma was played out. The same stories were told over and over again. The deep and shameful trauma. The abuse. The writhing self-hate. The hopeless shame that comes when love is just a fucking word that the abuser uses to gain control and keep control. “Do you know how much I love you?” said the father to his son. “Do you know how much I love you?” and then the father would show his “love” in the form of intimidation and name-calling and more threats of violence, and posturing, and shaming, and more name-calling. Then, when his son was collapsed, heaped on the floor crying. The father returned with more love. More violent posturing and shaming.  More name calling! Then more shame! The father smashed his head into a door repeatedly to get the attention that he so desperately needed. The attention that he deserved! The attention that he never got as a child. “Do you know how much I love you, son!?!?” his father cried repeatedly as he smashed his head into the door, in very much the same way that the clown from the Stephen King movie “IT” had done in the picture that the middle-aged-man agreed to see with his daughter for her birthday. He was not that much for horror films, honestly. But there it was right there on that huge fucking screen. It was played out for him right there, larger than life, just as his father had appeared to him all those years ago. That’s what the young man’s life was like. That is the love that he had known. Kind of like the love of the clown in that movie, IT, by Stephen King when he’s smashing his head through that glass repeatedly. The crushing of his own skull so that he can feed on the little boy that’s behind that glass, in that maze of mirrors. Yip. There it was. The trauma would find its way back. No matter how good you tried to be. No matter how good a boy you are. The clown is gonna fuck you. The clown is gonna get you. “There’s no fucking way out of this maze boy. You are mine! I own you. I FUCKING LOVE YOU!!! Cant’ you see that, son? Can’t you see how much I love you. I’m sorry son. I didn’t mean to treat you that way. Comer over here. Let me hold you. Let me hold you son. I love you. I love you. And what does the son do. The son who has never been loved truly. The son who is starving for exactly what the father is starving for. He returns into the arms of the clown who is now hovering over the boys neck with drooling fangs, because he can’t help himself. “Yes, boy. This is the love that I always needed. The great ophidian. The one who devours us whole and will shit us out the other end if we are willing.

It took 13.8 billion years for consciousness to evolve to a place where it could look back on itself and agree to hold space for exactly what-is. 13.8 billion years for consciousness to willingly take a death walk, to willingly agree to the death of the false-self, the death of the flesh, the death of the more shallow aspects of its being, in order that a deeper consciousness could arise. The Dying God
The old man waited patiently in the jungle clearing. White robes,  flowing beard—a dying God—waiting for the man who had much to do with his imminent demise. Sounds of struggle emanated from the jungle brush just beyond the perimeter of the clearing. Using his staff, the old man lowered himself onto a large fallen tree. The disturbance in the underbrush grew nearer. 
Finally, a figure arose from the multitude of wide leaves. And there she stood, just having emerged from the bush. Se was a troubled woman in her mid-thirties—victorian skirts, disheveled hair wilted from humidity, face stained by dirt. She panted from her exertion. She stood there for a moment, relieved to be free from the forest from which she’d just emerged. Then, she scanned the clearing; her eyes met the old man’s. 
“My Lord?” she said, as she stumbled to stand before him.
“Yes, daughter,” He said.
She crumbled at his feet. Her eyes were now fixed on the patterns in her skirt. Tears began as silent, intermittent convulsions in her torso. Then, deep sobs arose from her chest. Her face contorted.  Her eyes rose again to meet the old man’s gaze. Her mouth cracked open in tight expression of grief and thin strands of saliva stretched between her upper and lower lips. She remained there for quite some time. Her breathing steadied as her eyes met His. 
She raised herself slowly to her knees. Then she allowed her torso to collapse into the old man’s lap, hugging his abdomen. His hands naturally came to her head in an effort to comfort.
The two remained like this for a long moment as birds chattered and screeched in trees overhead.
“Emma?” said the old man, “Where is Charles?”
“He would not come,” she said. “His stomach is troubling him, and he is filled with anxiety at the thought of seeing you.”
“That is understandable,” said the dying God. “Emma, sit with me.”
Emma lifted herself from the old man’s lap and sat beside him now. She slumped, but she supported herself.
“All Gods must die Emma. It is how it has always been, and how it will always be. You know this to be true. I am merely the projection of what cannot be held in one form. I am only one projection of G_d, one image who points to that which as ALL.”
Emma noticed that a small group of chimpanzees had gathered around them. An adolescent chimp approached the old man and jumped up in his lap. The old man looked thoughtfully into the primate’s eyes. The young chimp’s mother sat down in front of Emma, offering her curled hand. Emma could somehow sense the motherliness in this creature that seemed so horrifyingly familiar in form to herself—hands, eyes, feet, and breasts.
“I am the God of metaphor, Emma, the God of story. Just as all life has changed over time, so do our Stories. This form that you see now, this form that you practice, this lense through which you see life, must pass away to make room for a less…how should I say? A less fatherly figure? Less fatherly, Emma, but not to exclude the Father. The mother is rising Emma. The mother needs to be known if your species is to continue on its path of transmutation. I know that it is difficult for you to understand. I see that you are dying a death. I know that you are hurting. I see you, child. I see you. Let us rest there for a moment. Will you rest there for a moment with me? I see you Emma….Rest with me here for a moment. Let me hold you…
There is a long pause (a menopause)...Emma cries….Emma sobs...She begs for this to be taken from her...She knows this is more than she can hold...She is held by the spirit of this being that is passing into new form.
Being speaks…. “This death that you are dying is still the way of the cross, Emma. It is still the way that you have been shown. But, the way that you see me is changing. Your very perception of who I am is transmuting, if you will. This image is evolving, just as all forms have evolved before me. Novel forms are created from this process. You, my daughter are a novel form. You, my daughter, are being born again. Your species is being born again every moment. Without an understanding of this evolution, humanity cannot transcend the binary. Without this understanding the human species is trapped in the delusion of good and evil, trapped in a static prison. 
This evolutionary understanding is a result of the birth of the age of reason. Spiral dynamics. The serpent which spirals toward the infinite center of the sun and is drawn infinitely deeper and deeper into this consciousness. Your species is not static. Life is not static. Life is like a thundercloud changing, and ever changing. Without this understanding it is very difficult to experience the One-ness of all life. 
Your husband has discovered a key to unlocking the door to a much broader room, a more expansive field of consciousness. There will be those who take this message and turn it in to something that is not. There will be those who will say that Charles is a heretic. He will be mocked and hated by some for many many years to come, but this is the promise being fulfilled for those who choose to embrace the deepest callings. This is the very heresy that brings your species into a deeper communion with who I really AM. Just as Christ was a heretic, so are the ones who carry the light after him.
It is no different with you, Emma. You are carrying this. You have said yes to your husband and you have said yes to life. He has carried this as far as it will go. It is coming Emma. There is no stopping it. If it is not Charles, it will be someone else. The message of the prophet must amplify the One-ness in the ears of the people. The message of the true prophet recognizes all as ONE and the one as part of the ALL.

Day 3...8:56AM
The middle-aged man was, once again, standing at the marble island in the kitchen of the adobe house on the Eastern High Plains. Seventeen years ago, the sky the sky was filled with red dust in this town where the man still lived and died. 
The man heard Dan G, his roomate making his way down the stairs. He was talking on his telephone by way of his headphones, dressed in his heavy, black jacket, kind of gliding along as he always seemed to do. Dan ended his conversation with his cousin, Dee. 
“Going for a walk?” said the middle-aged man. 
“Yes, sir.” said Dan.
“Well, I’ll go with you. Just let me get my jacket and some shoes.”
They got in Dan’s white Chevy Malibu and made the short drive to the track
They talked as they walked. The air was brisk. The golden grass on the infield of the track glimmered with frozen-white sparkling dew. The two men both proclaimed the walk a prayer for Dan’s health. Dan was concerned about his weight and the lack of physical activity in his life. The two friends reveled in one another’s company, as they always did when they had time together. 
Dan was now improvising quasi-Shakespeare-pentameter while the middle-aged man practiced his Irish accent, of which Dan was his teacher. They walked on the oval track for twenty minutes, renewing their friendship and proclaiming their undying love for one another. 
As they finished their walk. Dan collected a blue prayer flag from the track in remembrance of the prayer for health that they’d made together. They returned to the great adobe house in the Universal white Malibu. 
The middle-aged-man prepared oatmeal, as Dan NEVER cooked! They ate breakfast, trading inspiration, revelation, and much joy between themselves. They considered the hoi polloi. They watched building 7 fall again, that forgotten archive of New York City’s 9/11. They considered how the human species might suffer a death of the macro-ego. And finally, the Cliffs of Moher (More) where so many people had cast themselves into the sea to meet their own end. 
This was the usual gravity of their conversations. They were not men of shallow nature. Not today, at least. Not today, dear reader! Today they were alive and full of piss and vinegar! HaHa!
The middle aged man invited Dan to read Darwin’s prophecy. Dan read, then it was time for him to go. He had an appointment with his girlfriend. Before the two men parted each other’s company, they hugged one another as they recited the serenity prayer. This was their tradition. It had been some time since the middle-aged man had been to an AA meeting, it took him a moment to catch up with the prayer.
The writer returned to his work of writing in the Universal kitchen.
“Who is this?” Wondered the writer as he read the following poem. “It looks like Hafiz to me,” he responded to himself, “but we didn’t make a note of it, did we?” Forgive us, dear reader. We believe it to be Hafiz as translated by Ladinsky…with no title. Oh, please excuse us, dear reader.

Day 3….7:21PM
The middle-aged man stood, once again, in the great kitchen. The son had set on the world outside. Three lights burned brightly over marble island.  The writer moved three, thick, blue books clockwise around the marble slab island. He could now see himself in a great mirror. He now faced North into the great kitchen’s Universal Mirror. He faced the mirror in the North, the direction of the generative, nurturing adult according to a Bill Plotkin book that he’d read half of, Wild Mind. The writer now faced North into the great mirror. He now witnessed himself writing. 
He breathed. The man in the mirror breathed and looked deeply into his own figure. Black rimmed glasses. Overgrowing beard (which his mother hated). He was thin. He looked tired. He looked hungry somehow. A little bewildered. Confused? He was reminded of how his face had shifted forms before him in this same mirror as he’d eaten the mushrooms that first time, showing him that he was not nearly as solid as he once believed himself to be. He was not solid, he was more like a thunderhead, constantly in flux.
The man in the mirror felt his fingers curl as they hovered over the keyboard, ready for their next destination. The man in the mirror embraced the miracle that already was. Then he backspaced over several words to correct a mistake.
He was finding himself in some kind of natural cycle. “Is this a writers cycle?” he wondered to himself. “It suits me,” he said out loud. And it did suit him on that day. For instance, he had fallen asleep just two-and-a-half hours before, holding himself, and somehow being held, as he was unable to find any comfort from Netflix. He was also unable to find any comfort from Eli, who, several times, scratched the middle-aged man on the nose and cheeks as if he’d wanted something that could not be given. And it was true, the man had nothing to give to the cat except himself. The man admittedly observed himself wanting something form the cat that he could not seem to extract, a comfort that he could not quite find in the petting of his fur. “Everybody’s got a hungry heart,” thought the man to himself, “Cat’s and people alike.”
When he awoke from his short nap he felt as if he might have slept all night. But it was only 7:00PM, which he discovered as he cracked open the chromebook. The man wondered about the voices in his writing from the day before. He wondered about moving from past to present tense and jumping for third to first person. These were the concerns of the one who had been married to an English teacher for twenty years. This writer who was born to die for his dear reader’s birth.
He thought about Dave. A more recent writer in his life. Dave had encouraged him before Eileen’s email. They’d had several meaningful email exchanges, in which Dave was encouraging the writer. Eileen’s communication had come with power that would not have been possible without the groundwork that Harbor Dave had laid. 
The writer stood at the kitchen island in his olive drab coat that he’d bought at Wal-Mart for his poorly planned hithhiking adventure. He observed himself in all humility, facing North toward the generative-nurturing-adult. He observed the present tense pushing into a narrative being told in the past. He breathed in. He breathed out. “Is that what I need?” wondered the author. “Another title? A label? A descriptor? A profession?” Because that’s what he was feeling like now. He was feeling like a writer, an author, a man with a job to do. A man with a calling. A man with a purpose, because these words, this project, he felt was living through him now. This project had become the pulse of his life.
And because he was on medical leave, he had all the space to allow this to happen. Because he lived at Dan’s house rent free he had a safe and warm space to allow this Life to emerge. 
The Universal heater kicked on to warm the great adobe home.
North, the direction of the generative, nurturing, adult. He’d written a letter, upon Bill Plotikin’s direction. It was a love letter from the generative, nurturing adult to himself. 
The writer wondered if he could find it in his google drive. He located the file. He opened it. He cut and pasted it, acknowledging that the author was not disappearing in this moment. “Love never comes the same twice,” said the middle aged man to himself. “The miracle never happens the same twice,” he said joyfully as he accepted the sense of honesty that he was experiencing with himself right now, in the present tense. And he realized that he truly was nurturing himself in this moment.

The man’s next journey started after a night of travail. He lay in anguish on the bathroom floor for much of the night, which resulted in a text to Dan, “I know why Cliff is dead. I know why Chek keeps drinking.” That’s when he ingested the medicine.

Hours later, the middle-aged-man thought the experience was over. He crawled into bed. A red, fleece blanket served as the top layer of insulation. The heater blew, keeping the cabin cozy. He crawled under the covers. Then he saw something. 
It was there…
On the red blanket.
It was a miller mother. It had been crushed. It was severely injured. There was moth dust all around its suffering body. He had, assumedly, crushed this moth. He was the one who had caused this suffering that he saw before him.
The man looked down upon this moth which rested in a valley on this red blanket, and he saw that the moth was suffering deeply. The way that one of his antennas convulsed, he may as well have been screaming in agonizing pain. He was reaching out to the man. The man moved his right index finger toward his trembling antennae. As his index finger approached the moth it became clear to him that there was nothing he could do. In fact, any attempt to intervene would only make things worse for the moth.
Since the man was a child, it had been his habit to put suffering animals out of their misery. He felt that it was somehow his duty. There was a long list of animals with whom he had interacted in this way. But this time was different. He was not going to try to help this Moth out of this world. The man was going to bear witness to his suffering. He knew that he would stay with the moth for as long as it took. “Will it be hours?” he wondered. “What if I have to stay here until morning?” he thought. “This could take an entire day.” But he stayed.
He withdrew his right index finger from the moth and he began to simply witnesss. He watched as the moth began to crawl, almost imperceptibly slow up the canyon in the red blanket. As he watched the moth in it’s agonizing journey, he somehow became the Moth. Ant the moth became the Christ. It just was. 
And the man can never know how long he watched the Christ crawling up that valley. But the man knew exactly what he was witnessing. He was witnessing what had already happened and what would happen again innumberable times until we all understood. The man was witnessing that which does not demand attention. The man was witnessing that which does not insist upon an audience. He was witnessing the ONE that takes no offense when attention is not given. He was witnessing the ONE who forgives. He was witnessing the consciousness that arose from deep within us all. This was the consciousness that arose from the depths. This was the form of consciousness that looked down from his cross and said the un-speakable. This was the one who chose to forgive, despite the deep convulsions and revulstions that he experienced on the cross. The dying author (the one who was trying to find his own death so that his reader may live) sat in the living room of the southwestern-style adobe house. “What are those orangey-pink Mexican tiles called? They have a cool name,” the writer questioned of himself.
It was those large, pinkish-orange mexican style tiles which were currently providing the context for the living room in which the dying author sat, fingers curved patiently over home-row. 
Georgia O’keefe prints hung above, flanking the large fireplace on either side; a cattle skull and a morning glory, a wide river bordered by a scrub brush hill, a blue mountain on the desert horizon. You know, Georgia? Do you not dear reader? Please picture her now.

The dying author ventured out for a walk with the sunrise. He crunched through the golden, frozen grass in his brown, leather, slip-on loafers. Inside Stone
                          “The child who broke
                The one who woke up crying
                A lovely journey…”
                        —Book of the Ageless Ophidian, Chapter 9 v15
                                translated by Chogyam Trin Pan                                
In the thick air of a cool basement, two boys faced one another. They unzipped, engaging each other in a playful sword fight of sorts. The sun’s rays angled in through a half hazed window. 
“We need to get some girls down here,” says the taller of the two. 
A disturbance causes the smaller boy to turn quickly and face the slowly arcing dust motes traveling through the white light. The sound of the opening door from the top of the stairs jump-starts the two boy’s already elevated heart rates. Stairs creaking under feet, the small boy’s grandma chides sharply, “I know what you two are doing down there, and if you don’t stop right now I’m going to tell your fathers!”
The old woman stops half way down the closed stairwell. She stares at the boys who have just barely escaped being caught with their pants down. Trying to look innocent, not knowing now what to do with his hands, the small boy averts his eyes from his grandmother’s silhouette, now analyzing the cobwebs in the corner. The oldest boy stands awkwardly wide-eyed, breathing heavily through his open mouth, staring at the woman’s feet. 
Only now, under her gaze, does the little boy grasp the gravity of his innocent play. He only knows that he does not want his dad to know. The tight faced woman with the tautly wound beauty-shop curls forces the long silence into eternity as her eyes move from one boy to the other—the boys, defenseless against those pursed-lips.
Later, the younger boy found himself. In his grandfather’s quarter acre lot, he weaved his way through stacks of railroad ties, fence sections, camper tops, and rusting livestock trailers. His curiosity renewed—the sunshine and smell of sheep shit freeing him from the pressing weight of the concrete cellar and his grandmother’s threats. He made his way to the red fence at the back of the lot—the calling of birds and the singing cicadas now the only voices in his head. He unlatched the chain on the large swinging gate, climbed the rocky embankment to the tracks, and followed the rails to the wooden Santa Fe bridge.
He chose three grey rocks from the rail bed, as many as his seven year old hands could carry, and ventured out on to the wooden planks. The creek below came in to view through the gaps under his feet. He reassured himself that the space between the ties was narrow enough that he could catch himself if he were to lose his footing. As he approached the bridges’ center, directly over the rainbowed surface of an oily stagnating pool of water, he straddled one of the gaps and dropped a stone. In simple silence it fell for what may have been a second or perhaps much longer, a trick of time the boy held too tightly. He wished his hands were big enough to carry a thousand stones.
The rock broke the filmy surface of the pool…
He was sorry he had killed the baby bird. It hadn’t gone as expected. He had killed adult birds with his BB gun before, their glistening black and purple feathers ruffling as their neck and legs collapsed under the weight of their own body. That made him feel strong and respected, like a hunter. But the bare baby bird was different. He knew, from watching TV,  that it was his duty to put that little creature out of its misery. It was suffering. In fact, he relished the responsibility. The idea of it made him feel so grown up and wise, so responsible. “It is the right thing to do,” he said, relishing the serious and morbid nature of his task. That tiny naked creature, fallen from her nest, screeched and squirmed under the pressure of the curved x-acto blade on its neck. Half way through the surprisingly sinewy flesh, perplexed and horrified, the boy felt the warm red blood on his hands, but the baby would not die. The boy panicked. He stood facing the bird on the altar for a moment, dirt and leaves on his knees. Without the heart to complete the ceremony, he ran, leaving the pitiful writhing life form still squirming on the brick altar. He pushed open the screen door on the back porch, ran inside the two story brick house, and clamored quickly up the stairs to his mother’s room. She was folding laundry. He cried in her arms. The boy was loved for his sensitivity.
From his perch on the bridge, the boy dropped the second rock. Another moment of silence. He could hear his breath hovering over the chasm between himself and the water below. It was that space that held his attention, that quiet moment between release and splash down…
He had once imagined a stone so smooth that it couldn’t be held. Actually, he hadn’t as much imagined the smooth stone, as much as it had appeared in his being. The perfect creamy surface of this stone always contracted into a shadowy, craggling, painful object. Too terrible to touch. Sometimes, if he kept his eyes closed, he could witness this transformation over and over again; the hypnotizing change was out of his control. The little boy could not understand the aliveness of the stone in his vision, or why he was unable to control its transformation.
 He released the third rock. It strayed from its intended course and glanced off the sticky, tarred surface of the tie. The boy lost sight of it and carelessly repositioned his feet so that, with his eyes, he could follow the descent of the falling stone. Losing his footing with the wind, he connected himself to the silence again for a brief moment. He could hear the stone dancing on the rocks below as he regained his balance. His heart came into his his chest with loud thumps that he could feel in his ears. 
That night the boy lay in bed knowing that he could not go to school the next day. This knowing was manifested in a physical sensation that he would one day call dread; it was uncontrollable, like the smooth stone’s transformation into something untouchable. 
If he could make himself vomit his parents would have to let him stay home. He walked to the bathroom and shoved a finger down his throat but was unable to produce any substance from his stomach. He gagged as loud as he could and then plopped down heavily onto the cold white tile by the toilet, hoping his parents would hear his distress, angered by his general state of physical well-being. Wishing for disease, he recalled the stone’s hushed descent. It comforted him for one moment before the image of his grandmother returned like a chronic illness. Several more failed attempts at throwing-up produced pitiful gurgling sounds, causing his father to yell from upstairs, “You ARE going to school tomorrow!” The boy gave up on the process, hoisted himself from the floor, slumped his shoulders and plodded back to his bed.
He lay on his back, pulled the covers up to his chin, and focused his attention on the cracks in the ceiling. He sensed the rise and fall of his chest. Again he thought about the pocked stones, the tracks, the bridge, the dirty rainbow covering the foul waters. He perceived the weightlessness of the rock in the moment before it broke the surface. He stopped the descent in mid air, hovering himself in that space below the bridge. He became the stone’s mind.
His breathing slowed. Hands and feet buzzed. His limbs retreated. Eyes became black circles. Scaled skin slid under sheets. He lowered his long thick body from the soft bed to the scarred hardwood floor, curving along, past the bathroom tiles and up the stairs. His parents were sleeping. He paused for a moment as he reached the open door, surprised by his tongue as it slipped from his mouth; he could taste his parent’s breath and sweat in the air, hanging thick. He slid forward now, under their bed. He quickly curved his body around the hanging blankets, up and over his father’s chest, under sheets, and around his mother’s radiating leg. Entwined with the two, he rested, perfectly still, perfectly silent, his scaled skin detecting what had before been unknowable. He remained there for the time it takes a stone to fall. Then, as quickly and quietly as he had come, he unwound himself from their unconscious bodies and lowered his body onto an oval rug.
The reticulated form found its way to the laundry chute and spiraled down the smooth walls to the cellar where it curled in a corner next to the water heater, motionless, in a deep reptilian meditation, breathing long slow breaths—breaths that were very much like the

Patrimony
                    “Ophidian friend
                    Deepest reptilian brain
                    He eats the children…”
                        —Book of the Ageless Ophidian, Chapter 12 v42
                                                      translated by Chogyam Trin Pan
Although he and his friend never returned to the basement, he suspected that his grandmother had told on him anyway. His father was not a religious man, but he did preach fervently against the dirty butt-fuckers who soiled the earth with their flaming feminine accents. Untouchables. the most despised of humanity. The homos. The faggots. 
The boy willingly sang in his father’s angry choir while often suspecting himself to be just such an abomination. There had been the cellar; and sometimes there were daydreams, uncontrollable, like the contraction of the smooth stone in his mind, the thoughts playing over and again in a disturbingly persistent loop. The more the boy tried to stop his thoughts, the more powerful became the feedback frequency. 
At eleven years old he anxiously awaited puberty, frequently inspecting his underarms and scrotum for signs of any growth. He patrolled his slender legs for traces of coarse hair, and imagined his penis longer and darker. Nothing happened. From quick sideways glances stolen at the urinals he knew that he was behind everyone else. While changing after gym class, some of the boys began to proudly display their primal hardware. He sensed that these more mature boys were altogether different creatures, full of  confidence produced by their impressive physical change. They were men. Terrified by their deepened voices and superior strength, he shamefully shielded his own paltry penis. He knew that he needed more if he was ever going to start fucking girls. All these thoughts, sad and shameful secrets.
The boy’s mother provided him with a sex-education book. He poked and prodded, hoping to achieve the elusive orgasm he read about. It all felt good, but no liquid. Once he could produce semen, he hoped things would change. He put on cologne and hungered for the attention of the prettiest girls. He envied the confidence of the popular boys. They had courage. It was evident in the way they moved and laughed; they were obviously animated by some mysterious force. He wanted them to talk to him. He wanted to be them.
It scared him how much he wanted them. Their smooth confidence aroused his desire and increased the frequency of his unwanted daydreams. He forgot about them sometimes, but they always came back. The fear that these fantasies produced was paralyzing. On the bus ride home from school he shut his eyes tightly to lock down the tears. The warm sun flickered from behind the trees and bounced behind his eyelids. He was afraid of what he knew was the truth, that he was a fag. 
When the boy ran with flopping wrists his father showed him how to clench his fists. When the boy was threatened at school, the father advised him to go ape-shit-crazy on his enemies. The father tried to show his son in so many ways how to be a man, but it wasn’t having any effect. The boys own father, in fact, was not quite sure of his own manhood. But the boy did not know that. The boy knew that he was not a man like his father. It was Fall and the boy was still bothered by a fantasy he’d had last spring involving a baseball teammate. 
At the movie theater he was surprised when he sat in the back row with a beautiful girl from his class. They kissed until their lips were red and puffy. Although elevated by the rapture of their mutual consent, the wetness of her lips, the smell of their mixed saliva, her smooth skin, and proof of his own heterosexuality, he broke up with her the next day at school, embarrassed by her name, Tanda. He had loved the little girl that night at the movies, so beautiful, so willing, so present, so generous with her attention. He loved her even as he cut her off by the lockers. She cried. But her name sounded so black. So embarrassing. Tanda.
He aimed hateful language at minority classmates, calling Tony, the only black kid in his grade, a walking-tootsie-roll. Afterward, Tony told Michael, “I wanna tear off my skin so I can be white!” 
His father hated the towel-heads at the university because they whistled at white women.  So, the boy had names for them too. He called his classmate, Behrang, an Iranian-Turd, or just “IT,” for short. 
“If you call me that name one more time, I am going to hit you,” Behrang said to the boy. 
The boy mindlessly rose to Behrang’s challenge, repeating the insult immediately, straight to his face. Behrang, the strong young Iranian, dropped his shoulder, shifted his weight, and applied the torque of his torso to deliver a precise punch to the boy’s guts, forcing his breath out through an opened mouth. Behrang walked away and the boy fell to the dry, red Oklahoma dirt, his neck bleeding under the sharp pressure of an invisible blade, writhing on the little bird’s altar. 
Scales formed in the dust. The snake struck, constricted, consumed the little bleeding bird, then she coiled into the recesses of the playground wall built from railroad ties, protected from the wind, warmed by the sun. The boy was digested slowly over many following years, the nutrients from his skin, muscles, organs, and bones metabolized by  the ageless ophidian, his friend.

The tenderness presents itself…today…now
The unknown…
The pain of youth…
The musician now stood in the living room playing a conga drum. It was a dark red conga, one of a pair that ex-wife (mother of his children) had given him for Christmas. The drum now resided in the living room of the impressive adobe house. The man stood on the pink-orange mexican tiles playing the conga drum. There was a shaman residing in the living room as well. A native American Eagle priest lived in the recess of the wall. 
As the musician played the drum, he began to vocalize. He beat the drum faster and faster, and harder and harder. And as his rhythm and intensity increased, so did the volume and emotional content of his vocalizations. In the musicians heart was anguish--Visions of the pain of his youth. Remembrances of when all of this--the feminine arising from within-- would have been unacceptable. The drummer’s beat and vocalizations came to a climax, leaving him in tears, in uncertainty, and grief (is that what it was?). But, wherever this wave was taking him, he felt that he was preparing for the journey. He suspected that he had been suffering all of his life because of his inability to accept what was now rising up from within.
The wildy-talented-writer had stayed up until 4AM the night before, editing the first chapters of his project. He was starting to see a through-line. The distress call, the feminine offering her help in the struggle? 
“Is that the through line?” wondered the writer. “It is about the feminine, yes? But not just the feminine, right? The writer gives way to the possibility that this is not going to turn him into his father’s nightmare.”
“Hmmmmm. That’s interesting,” the Great mother gently responded with genuine curiosity. “Which father’s voice was that that just spoke? Is it okay if I help you out, right now? I have heard you asking for my help. I have heard you praying for my insight.”
“Yes, Great Mother, I would love to hear from you. Please shine your light on my being. Speak to me in a way that my heart understands, Mother.”
“I am shining my light on you now, my son. You will come into this wisdom. We will stay connected. We are connected. We are One, you and I son.”
And with that, the author did feel his heart filled with a gentle kindness, which felt very different in the man’s chest than the mind-fuck that he was in before. The voice in which the (angry) scared father arises.
“That’s good, said the Great Mother, you were willing to see him as scared instead of angry. And you prayed for your father tonight in song, didn’t you, my Son?”
“Yes, mother. I had a genuine song of healing for the man. It was truly a miracle.”
The writer paused. He breathed. He nodded to the vipassana, allowing himself the space to trust his body, to hear the voice of God in his breath. Praise be to Y-w-h, the unspeakable name of the ONE. Praise be to the I AM, which we ARE.
The disappearing author recalled a recurring dream that he’d had when he was in his early twenties. A dream in which he woke up, crawled out of bed, went to the mirror to brush his teeth. When the young man saw himself in the reflection he was terrified. “A green lizard,” is what the young man called what he’d seen. The young man had the dream twice. And It was powerful medicine in his heart, and much needed, for the young man was unable to make peace in his own heart.
The wildly talented writer sat in the living room writing .
“Why does he keep bringing up the ‘wildlytalented writer’ thing?”said the writer. 
“Why? Is it to show his ego working with some big expectation of himself?” said the middle-aged-man. 
The writer stayed with his work. He felt a story coming on again. It was a story that he’d told many times before. He was unsure now of how to tell it again. Or even why he should tell it again. “I will try telling the story in its simplest form,” he thought to himself, “That would be a different way to approach it. 
“You could allow me to help, if you’d like,” offered the mother.
“Oh yes, Mother! Thank you so much for interjecting here,” said the writer. “I would very much like your help.”
And so it came to pass the simplest version of his story was told:
There was a traumatized boy who grew into a traumatized young man. This young man’s suffering went back for generations. The young man was unable to make peace in his own heart. He was greatly troubled. The Universe reached out to him. He responded. He was miraculously reconciled to the natural goodness of his own being, his deepest Self. The young man began experiencing the world in novel ways. His heart soared. 
A young traumatized woman who was also experiencing the evolution of life in novel forms saw this young man. Her heart rejoiced in him. They went for coffee together, where she listened to the young man speak from the joy of his new salvation. The young man had never been listened to so deeply. 
The young man’s heart had recently been broken by another woman. He never wanted to feel that way again. He sensed that this new young woman would never leave him. And he was right. What he had sensed was this young woman’s deep fear of abandonment because of her trauma. It was true, her trauma would make it impossible for her to leave the man, no matter how miserable together they might become. So, the man got what he thought he needed, a woman who would never leave him.
“Hello, Mother?”
“Hello, Son.” 
“Would you read that last paragraph with me and show me what you think?”
After reading the last paragraph, the Mother had a question, “ So the young man did not want to hurt?”
“Yes, Mother. He did not want to hurt.”
“And the young man felt like he knew that she would never leave him?”
“Yes, Great Mother, the middle-aged-man distinctly remembers ‘knowing’ that she wouldn’t leave.”
“That is interesting,” she hummed. “Let me ask you this, Son? Do you feel like she should have left you? Do you feel somehow that you deserved to be left?”
“Yes, Great Mother, I did somehow feel that I was the lesser of the two of us. I watched myself screw up so many times. I watched my heart stray from her. I watched myself getting depressed and angry. I yelled at the kids. I hurt the dogs. I couldn’t seem to make myself happy. I kept falling in love with other women. It was really confusing. I so often felt that I didn’t love her—not all the time—but often. “
“I do remember times when things were good between us. I remember looking back on our history together and being grateful that we were still together. I truly felt and appreciated her strengths. I blessed those strengths in her as much as possible. She worked so hard to get herself through school. It was one of the most incredible things I’ve ever seen in my life. I could often admire her strength…So, Mother?”
“Yes, Son?”
“Mother, I noticed that when you asked me if I felt that I deserved to be left, I started making a list of those bad things that I did. And then I made a list of  some of the good things that I did?”
“Yes, Son. That is what you did. Why do you suppose that you might have done that?
“Why do I do that, Mother?” Said the Son? Is it because I have a hard time experiencing the natural inner-goodness of  my being? So I try to justify my value by my deeds?”
“Hmmm…I think I like the way that you said that, Son,” said the mother.
“Mother?”

I need this for my health. I want to be present in this world in deeper ways. I want to stop spreading my trauma around to others. Mother? I need your help. I cannot do this for myself.”
And so it came to pass that the Mother answered the middle-aged-man’s prayer. She was in dialogue with her son. 
Thought the writer: I am so grateful. Mother is so kind. I like the way she asks me questions and allows her wisdom to rise up into me. As her love and wisdom rises up in me, I am able to answer the questions that she asks. She is very calm. She is very helpful. She is quiet in my heart. I am so happy to sing her praises. I can hear her in the wind outside my window now. Thank you, Mother, for this sweet interaction between myself and you.”
The writer now continued the most Universal story. He asked his mother to keep watch over his heart. 
“I am coming to trust our Great Mother,” thought the writer before continuing on.
The young man wanted a family. He believed it would make him whole. He did his best to trust God’s leading at every step in his pursuit of the his wholeness.
He pursued the young woman. She had a vision. She believed that he could complete her (or at least that’s how she interpreted the vision that she’d had). The young couple quickly got married. They had three children. However, the couple found that they were unable to fit themselves into a traditional mold. They flipped their house over. The woman became the main bread winner. 
Sitting by a fountain one day, their youngest daughter in a stroller, they consciously switched their allegiance from the church to the University. They became feminists. They learned of the oppressive patriarchy and they hated it. They swung from the Christian right to the progressive left, which the man eventually found to be less progressive than he’d hoped for (once again leaving behind form).
The man entered his age of reason, exploring logic until he saw how silly logic could be (Thanks Opal, “logic is silly. That’s all it took for him to see. Three simple words and the spell was broken). The man floated there at the edge of his observable Universe, facing the void, the meaninglessness. Determined to rid himself of all ignorance and archaic superstition, he scraped out his insides out with a cosmic melon baller. He became a militantly-minded atheist. He despised the weakness of those who needed religion. He could speak clearly about the dangers of fundamentalism. His heart emaciating. 
He began facing the nothingness of it all for hours at a time through meditation. He sat with the exact nothingness that everything was, accepting the absolute emptiness. He made peace with that perfectly (for brief periods). He stopped putting anything in his body that would harm him—drugs, alcohol, caffeine, sugar. He made beautiful peace with  a job that he did not want to be at.
But, no matter how hard the man worked to be okay, he continued breaking down at work. He was often miserable, no matter how hard he worked at accepting himself, no matter how much he resisted blaming other people and circumstances. The pilot was familiar with the field.  Over twenty years ago the pilot had sold everything so that he could buy that field. It was the field in which, so many years ago, he had unearthed a great treasure.
